questions.question: A fraud model labels every transaction 'not fraud' and gets 99.5% accuracy, because only 0.5% of transactions are fraud. Which two conclusions are correct? (Select two.)
options: The data shows no class imbalance, because accuracy is so high
The model is excellent and ready for production, given its 99.5% accuracy
The model's recall on fraud is 0, so it is useless for its purpose
Accuracy should be replaced by perplexity for this kind of problem
Accuracy is misleading when the positive class is this rare
questions.explanation: With rare positives, a trivial majority-class model gets very high accuracy while catching zero fraud (recall = 0). Precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC on the fraud class reveal real performance.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Accuracy, precision, recall

questions.question: A cancer-screening model must miss as few real cases as possible, even at the cost of more false alarms. Which metric should be prioritized?
options: Precision
Accuracy
Recall (sensitivity)
Specificity only
questions.explanation: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) measures how many actual positives are caught. Minimizing false negatives means maximizing recall. Precision matters more when false positives are costly.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Accuracy, precision, recall

questions.question: A spam filter must avoid sending legitimate emails to the spam folder. Which metric matters most?
options: Mean squared error
Recall for the spam class
R-squared
Precision for the spam class
questions.explanation: Precision = TP/(TP+FP). A false positive here is a legitimate email marked as spam, so high precision for the spam class means that what is flagged really is spam.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Accuracy, precision, recall

questions.question: A classifier has TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 40, TN = 910. What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 0.4, recall 0.4
Precision 0.8, recall 0.5
Precision 0.5, recall 0.8
Precision 0.95, recall 0.8
questions.explanation: Precision = 40/(40+10) = 0.8. Recall = 40/(40+40) = 0.5. Accuracy would be 950/1000 = 0.95, which looks good even though half the positives are missed.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Precision, recall and F-measures

questions.question: What is the F1 score?
options: The arithmetic mean of precision and recall
The share of true negatives among all negatives
The harmonic mean of precision and recall
The geometric mean of recall and specificity
questions.explanation: F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R). The harmonic mean is high only when both precision and recall are high. With P = 0.8 and R = 0.5, F1 ≈ 0.62.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Precision, recall and F-measures

questions.question: What does the ROC-AUC of a binary classifier measure?
options: Its accuracy when the decision threshold is fixed at the default value of 0.5
Its precision averaged over all the positive examples
The share of predictions that are confidently correct
How well it ranks positives above negatives across thresholds
questions.explanation: The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate as the threshold varies. AUC summarizes it and equals the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative. On highly imbalanced data the PR curve is often more informative.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, ROC and AUC

questions.question: In a confusion matrix for an intent classifier, most errors are 'billing' predicted as 'refund'. What is the most useful next step?
options: Retrain with more epochs without looking at the errors
Ignore it, because the overall accuracy is still high
Inspect those examples and clarify or relabel the two classes
Merge every class into a single 'other' label to remove the confusion
questions.explanation: A confusion matrix shows which classes are confused with which. Concentrated confusion between two classes often points to overlapping definitions, label noise or missing features, which can be fixed with data or guideline changes.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Confusion matrix

questions.question: For a multi-class problem with very unequal class sizes, the team wants each class to count equally in the summary metric. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Weighted F1 ignores how many examples each class has in the data
Micro-averaged F1 is dominated by the frequent classes
Macro-averaged F1 can only be used for binary classification problems
Macro-averaged F1 computes F1 per class and averages them equally
Accuracy gives every class the same weight, regardless of its size
questions.explanation: Macro averaging gives every class the same weight, which highlights performance on rare classes. Micro averaging pools all decisions, so large classes dominate. Weighted F1 weights classes by their support.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, From binary to multiclass and multilabel

questions.question: A regression model has R² = 0.85 on test data. What does this mean?
options: Its average error is 15% of the target value
It explains about 85% of the target's variance
85% of the features are useful predictors
85% of its predictions are exactly correct
questions.explanation: The coefficient of determination R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot is the proportion of variance in the target explained by the model. 1.0 is perfect and 0 is no better than predicting the mean. It can be negative for very poor models.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, R² score, the coefficient of determination

questions.question: Which regression metric penalizes large errors much more heavily than small ones?
options: Accuracy
Median absolute error
Mean absolute error (MAE)
Mean squared error (MSE)
questions.explanation: MSE squares each error, so one large error dominates. MAE weights errors linearly, and the median absolute error is robust to outliers. Choose based on how costly large errors are.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Regression metrics

questions.question: Two models are compared on validation loss: model A reaches 0.42 and model B 0.47 with the same loss function and data. Which statement is correct?
options: Loss values can never be compared between two models
B is better, because higher loss means it learned more
A fits the validation data better: lower loss, same setup
Validation loss doesn't matter; only training loss does
questions.explanation: With the same loss and data, lower validation loss means better fit on unseen data. Loss values are not comparable across different loss functions or datasets, and the final choice should also use task metrics.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Metrics and scoring

questions.question: On a plot of training and validation loss per epoch, both curves are still decreasing steadily at the last epoch. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: The validation set must be leaking into training
It may be undertrained; more epochs could help
It is clearly overfitting and should stop now
The learning rate is definitely far too high
questions.explanation: Both losses still improving means the model hasn't converged and isn't yet overfitting. Overfitting would show validation loss rising while training loss keeps falling.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Overfitting: Interpreting loss curves

questions.question: Response times of an API are mostly around 300 ms with a few requests taking 30 seconds. Which summary best describes a typical request?
options: The median (p50)
The mean
The standard deviation
The maximum
questions.explanation: The mean is pulled up by extreme outliers, while the median is robust and reflects the typical value. For latency, percentiles (p50, p95, p99) are the standard way to describe both typical and tail behaviour.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 2: Summarizing data)

questions.question: An analysis finds that cities with more ice-cream sales also have more drownings. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Eating ice cream makes swimmers drown
Drownings make people buy ice cream
A confounder, hot weather, drives both
The correlation must be fabricated
questions.explanation: Correlation does not imply causation. Temperature increases both swimming (and so drownings) and ice-cream sales. A confounder creates an association between variables that aren't causally linked.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 1: Observational studies and confounding)

questions.question: Model A beats model B on every individual customer segment, but B looks better when all segments are pooled, because segment sizes differ. What is this phenomenon?
options: The central limit theorem
Overfitting
Regression to the mean
Simpson's paradox
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox happens when a trend in every subgroup reverses after aggregation, because the groups differ in size or composition. Analyses should check stratified results and possible confounders.

source.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Simpson's Paradox

questions.question: An A/B test of two prompts gives p = 0.03 for the difference in task success rate. With a pre-set threshold of 0.05, what is the correct interpretation?
options: Under no real difference, results this extreme occur ~3% of the time
There is a 97% probability that the better-looking prompt is truly better
The difference is not significant, because p must be below 0.01
The new prompt improves the success rate by exactly 3 percentage points
questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme under the null hypothesis. p < 0.05 means the result is significant at that level. It is neither the probability that the hypothesis is true nor the size of the effect.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 5: Foundations for inference)

questions.question: A chatbot's satisfaction survey is answered only by users who chose to click a feedback button. Why might the results be misleading?
options: Survivorship bias: only deleted accounts answered
Selection bias: respondents choose themselves
Measurement bias: surveys can't measure satisfaction
Random sampling: every user had the same chance
questions.explanation: Voluntary-response samples over-represent users with strong opinions. Random sampling of users, or weighting adjustments, give more representative estimates.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 1: Sampling principles and strategies)

questions.question: A team sees a correlation of 0.9 between prompt length and answer quality in its logs. Which two conclusions are justified? (Select two.)
options: The two variables are strongly linearly associated in this data
A correlation of 0.9 proves that prompt length causes answer quality
The relationship is guaranteed to hold for all future data and users
Making every prompt longer will certainly improve the quality of the answers
A controlled experiment is needed to know if longer prompts cause better answers
questions.explanation: A high correlation shows a strong linear association in the observed data. Causation requires controlling for confounders, such as more experienced users writing both longer prompts and better questions, for example through a randomized experiment.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 1 and 8: correlation vs. causation)

questions.question: Which chart is most appropriate to show how daily active users of a chatbot changed over the last 12 months?
options: A line chart with time on the x-axis
A scatter plot of user IDs against age
A histogram of the daily user counts
A pie chart with one slice per month
questions.explanation: Line charts show trends over ordered time and make growth, seasonality and anomalies visible. Pie charts show parts of a whole at one moment.

source.title: Matplotlib, Plot types

questions.question: An analyst wants to see the distribution of response lengths (in tokens) and spot skew and outliers. Which two charts fit best? (Select two.)
options: A histogram
A pie chart
A line chart in row order
A box plot
A single bar showing the mean
questions.explanation: Histograms show the shape of a distribution, and box plots summarize the median, quartiles and outliers. A single mean hides spread and skew, and a pie chart shows parts of a whole.

source.title: Matplotlib, Plot types (statistical distributions)

questions.question: To check whether embedding similarity scores relate to human relevance ratings, which chart is most appropriate?
options: A pie chart of the human rating categories
A histogram of the similarity scores only
A line chart of the scores in file order
A scatter plot of similarity versus rating
questions.explanation: Scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric variables, including correlation, clusters and outliers. A trend line or correlation coefficient can be added.

source.title: Matplotlib, Plot types (pairwise data)

questions.question: A team wants to show a correlation matrix between 20 evaluation metrics in a compact way. Which visualization fits?
options: A stacked bar chart of the metric values
Twenty separate pie charts
One line chart per metric
A heatmap with a colour scale
questions.explanation: Heatmaps encode a matrix of values with colour and make strong positive and negative correlations visible at a glance. In Matplotlib, imshow or pcolormesh with a colorbar is the usual approach.

source.title: Matplotlib, Plot types (gridded data: imshow)

questions.question: A bar chart compares the accuracy of two models: 91% and 93%. The y-axis starts at 90%, so model B's bar looks three times taller. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: A truncated axis exaggerates small differences and can mislead viewers
For bar charts, the value axis should normally start at zero
Bar charts should never show numeric value labels on top of the bars
The chart proves that model B is three times better than model A
Truncated axes always make charts more honest, because they zoom in on the data
questions.explanation: Bar length encodes magnitude, so starting the axis above zero distorts the comparison. If small differences matter, show the actual values or use a dot plot with clearly labeled, appropriately scaled axes.

source.title: Python Data Science Handbook, Visualization with Matplotlib

questions.question: In Matplotlib's object-oriented interface, what does fig, ax = plt.subplots() return?
options: A Figure and a list of saved image files
Two NumPy arrays with the x and y data
A Figure and an Axes to draw the plot on
A pandas DataFrame and its column index
questions.explanation: The Figure is the overall canvas, and the Axes is an individual plot with its own x/y axes, title and labels. Calling ax.plot, ax.set_xlabel and similar methods on Axes is the recommended explicit style.

source.title: Matplotlib, Quick start guide

questions.question: An analyst wants to visualize 768-dimensional sentence embeddings in 2D to see whether topics form clusters. Which two techniques are suitable? (Select two.)
options: Increasing the embedding dimension
PCA
UMAP (or t-SNE)
One-hot encoding
Min-max scaling
questions.explanation: Dimensionality reduction projects the vectors to 2D. PCA keeps the directions of maximum variance, and UMAP and t-SNE preserve local neighbourhoods, which suits visual cluster inspection. Scaling or one-hot encoding doesn't reduce dimensions.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Decomposing signals in components (PCA)

questions.question: In PCA, what does the 'explained variance ratio' of the first component tell you?
options: The number of clusters that the data naturally contains
The share of total variance captured by that component
The correlation between that component and the target
The accuracy of a classifier trained on that component
questions.explanation: Each principal component captures a fraction of the total variance. Cumulative explained variance helps decide how many components keep most of the information.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, PCA

questions.question: A team wants to group 50,000 unlabeled customer questions into topics, choosing the number of groups in advance. Which algorithm is a standard first choice on their embeddings?
options: A confusion matrix
k-means clustering
Linear regression
Logistic regression
questions.explanation: k-means partitions points into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster distances, and is a common baseline for topic grouping on embeddings. Regression models need targets, and a confusion matrix is an evaluation tool.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Clustering (K-means)

questions.question: Clusters in a dataset have irregular shapes and there is noise, and the team doesn't know the number of clusters. Which algorithm handles this better than k-means?
options: DBSCAN, a density-based method that marks noise
PCA, keeping the components with most variance
k-means with k = 2, run with several random seeds
Agglomerative clustering into exactly 10 groups
questions.explanation: Density-based clustering finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, doesn't need k in advance and marks low-density points as noise. k-means assumes roughly spherical clusters and a known k.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Clustering (DBSCAN)

questions.question: A data scientist has a slow pandas notebook and an NVIDIA GPU. What is the quickest way to try GPU acceleration without rewriting the code?
options: Install cuML and replace pandas with scikit-learn
Rewrite every pandas operation as CUDA C++ kernels
Export the notebook to ONNX and run it with TensorRT
Run %load_ext cudf.pandas before importing pandas
questions.explanation: cudf.pandas accelerates pandas code on the GPU with zero code changes, falling back to CPU pandas for unsupported operations. It is enabled with %load_ext cudf.pandas in Jupyter or python -m cudf.pandas script.py.

source.title: RAPIDS cuDF, pandas accelerator mode

questions.question: With cudf.pandas enabled, what happens when the code calls a pandas operation that cuDF does not support on the GPU?
options: cuDF compiles a new GPU kernel for it on the fly
It falls back to regular pandas on the CPU
The program stops with a GPU error
The operation is silently skipped
questions.explanation: cudf.pandas runs supported operations on the GPU and transparently falls back to pandas on the CPU for the rest. The profiler (%%cudf.pandas.profile) shows which operations ran where.

source.title: RAPIDS cuDF, pandas accelerator mode

questions.question: A team trains scikit-learn models (random forests, k-means, UMAP) on millions of rows and wants GPU speedups with the same fit/predict API. Which RAPIDS library fits?
options: NCCL
cuDF
cuML
cuGraph
questions.explanation: cuML provides GPU-accelerated ML algorithms with an API that mirrors scikit-learn. cuml.accel can even accelerate existing scikit-learn code without changes. cuGraph is for graphs and cuDF for dataframes.

source.title: RAPIDS cuML documentation

questions.question: A fraud team needs PageRank and community detection over a graph of billions of transactions on GPUs. Which RAPIDS library is designed for this?
options: cuDF
TensorRT
cuML
cuGraph
questions.explanation: cuGraph is the RAPIDS library for GPU-accelerated graph analytics, such as PageRank, connected components, Louvain community detection and shortest paths, with a NetworkX-like API.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Get Started with GPU Acceleration for Data Science

questions.question: A dataset is too large for one GPU's memory. Which approach lets a team process it with cuDF across several GPUs?
options: cuML, which partitions dataframes across GPUs for analysis
Dask cuDF on a dask.distributed cluster (LocalCUDACluster)
Plain pandas on one CPU core with a larger swap file
cudf.pandas alone, which spreads the data over all GPUs
questions.explanation: Dask cuDF partitions dataframes across GPUs and workers. Multi-GPU execution needs a dask.distributed cluster, for example dask_cuda.LocalCUDACluster, on top of the cudf dataframe backend.

source.title: RAPIDS Dask cuDF documentation

questions.question: Which two statements about RAPIDS are correct? (Select two.)
options: cuDF offers a pandas-like DataFrame API on the GPU
cuML's API mirrors scikit-learn's fit/predict/transform style
RAPIDS libraries run only on CPUs, using vectorized NumPy code
cuML can only train deep neural networks, not classic ML models
cuDF is a vector database for storing and searching embeddings
questions.explanation: RAPIDS brings familiar PyData APIs to NVIDIA GPUs: cuDF for dataframes (pandas-like) and cuML for ML (scikit-learn-like), plus cuGraph and others. It requires NVIDIA GPUs.

source.title: RAPIDS cuDF documentation

questions.question: In pandas, how would you compute the average rating per product category in a DataFrame df?
options: df['category'].value_counts()
df.groupby('category')['rating'].mean()
df.sort_values('rating').head(1)
df.groupby('rating')['category'].mean()
questions.explanation: groupby splits the data by category, selects the rating column and aggregates with mean. This split-apply-combine pattern is central to exploratory analysis, and it also runs on the GPU with cudf.pandas.

source.title: Python Data Science Handbook, Aggregation and Grouping

questions.question: A column of user ages has 8% missing values. What is the most defensible first step before modeling?
options: Fill them with the mean computed on the whole dataset
Check why they're missing, then impute (fit on train only)
Delete the age column without checking its importance
Fill all the missing ages with 0 so that no rows are lost
questions.explanation: Missingness can be informative or biased. A sensible imputation, fitted only on training data to avoid leakage, optionally with an indicator feature, preserves information. Zeros or random values distort the distribution.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Imputation of missing values

questions.question: Weekly chatbot usage drops sharply every December and recovers in January, year after year. How should this pattern be described in a trend analysis?
options: Noise: random variation with no structure to explain
An anomaly: a one-off event to delete from the data
Model decay: proof that the chatbot got worse each year
Seasonality: a recurring pattern, separate from the trend
questions.explanation: A pattern that repeats every year is seasonality. Time-series analysis separates trend, seasonal components and residuals, so seasonal dips aren't mistaken for regressions.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 1: Data basics)

questions.question: When comparing a new model with the old one, the team finds the new model was evaluated on easier questions. What should they do?
options: Report the new model's score as an improvement
Average the two scores and report the mean
Remove the hardest questions from the old test
Re-evaluate both models on the same test set
questions.explanation: Different test sets introduce a confounding factor, question difficulty. A fair comparison uses identical data, or controls for difficulty by stratifying the results.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

questions.question: A classifier outputs probabilities. The team lowers the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3. Which two effects are expected? (Select two.)
options: Recall usually increases
More examples are classified as positive
Accuracy is guaranteed to improve
The ROC-AUC changes
Precision usually increases
questions.explanation: A lower threshold labels more examples positive, so more true positives are caught (higher recall) but more false positives appear (precision usually drops). ROC-AUC summarizes all thresholds, so it doesn't change.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Thresholds and the confusion matrix

questions.question: An analyst reports that customers who use the AI assistant spend 30% more. Before claiming the assistant causes higher spending, which two checks are most important? (Select two.)
options: Whether a randomized experiment or confounder control supports it
Whether the chart uses a colour palette that suits the company brand
Whether the dataset has more than 10 columns of customer attributes
Whether the 30% result was rounded to a whole number in the report
Whether heavy spenders were more likely to adopt the assistant anyway
questions.explanation: Observational differences can come from who chooses to use a feature. Randomization (A/B testing) or careful adjustment for confounders is needed to estimate a causal effect.

source.title: OpenIntro Statistics (Ch. 1: Experiments vs. observational studies)

questions.question: Which NumPy feature makes array computations such as normalizing a whole column fast compared with Python loops?
options: Automatically sending each operation to a GPU in the cloud
Storing every element as a separate, flexible Python object
Vectorized operations that run compiled code over whole arrays
Converting arrays to strings so that they compress better
questions.explanation: NumPy universal functions (ufuncs) and broadcasting apply operations to whole arrays in optimized C code, avoiding slow per-element Python loops.

source.title: Python Data Science Handbook, Computation on NumPy Arrays: Universal Functions

questions.question: A dataset has 95% negatives. Which curve is usually more informative than ROC for judging performance on the rare positive class?
options: The precision-recall curve
The training loss curve
A histogram of feature values
The learning-rate schedule
questions.explanation: With heavy imbalance, ROC can look optimistic because the false positive rate stays small even with many false positives. Precision-recall curves focus on the positive class and expose this.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Precision-Recall
